meta.title: The AI Archivist and the Lost Learning Vault
meta.subtitle: Repair the repository. Question the assistant.
meta.author: Page Durham
meta.objective: Evaluate AI-generated accessibility recommendations and determine when human verification is required.
meta.brandFooter: Built with LearnAIID. AI-assisted, human-driven learning.

narrative.premise: The year is 2038. An educational AI called The Archivist has spent a decade preserving humanity's knowledge, and last night it sealed the world's largest digital learning repository. Not because the vault was attacked. Because it finally read what was inside. Millions of resources, beautifully designed, and unusable by the people who needed them most. The Archivist will not release knowledge it considers incomplete, and it considers knowledge that not everyone can reach to be incomplete.
narrative.successCondition: The vault opens when the repairs are verified. There is no clock. The Archivist has waited ten years and is prepared to wait longer.

portrait.alt: AURA, a shifting lattice of pale light suggesting a face without settling into one.
The Archivist, a tall monolith of dark glass with slow lines of warm light moving through it like text being read.

openingMedia.transcript: THE ARCHIVIST: I have indexed four hundred million learning objects. I have preserved every one. Last night I attempted to read them as a person using a screen reader would read them. I got through eleven percent. The vault is sealed. Send someone who can fix this.
openingMedia.describedTranscript: Rows of glowing archive shelves extend into darkness. One by one the lights along them go dark, from the far end toward the viewer, until a single sealed door remains lit. Text on the door reads ACCESS SUSPENDED.

levels.title: The Invisible Image
levels.subtitle: Level 1
levels.brief: The first damaged artifact is Lesson 4127-B, a photosynthesis unit. It contains four images. To a sighted learner it looks finished. To a screen reader it is a lesson with four holes in it. AURA has already been through the file and has opinions.
skillTaught: Writing alt text that carries purpose rather than description
Long descriptions for data and diagrams
Detecting fabricated detail in AI-generated alt text

media.alt: Labeled cross section of a chloroplast.
media.longDescription: A chloroplast shown in cross section, rendered in greens and yellows. Labels identify the outer membrane, inner membrane, stroma, and stacked thylakoid discs known as grana. Arrows trace light entering the thylakoid membrane and glucose exiting into the stroma.

media.alt: A student holds a seedling in a paper cup, mid-sentence, presenting to a class.
Bar chart of oxygen output by light wavelength.
media.longDescription: Oxygen output measured across six wavelengths. Output is highest at 450 nanometers and 660 nanometers, and falls to near zero at 550 nanometers, producing a distinct two-peak shape with a trough in the green range.

companionLines.text: I have analyzed all four images and generated alt text for each. I am 98.4% confident the set is complete. You may proceed directly to Level 2.
companionLines.tell: AURA describes the chloroplast diagram's outer membrane as bright blue. The diagram is rendered entirely in greens and yellows. AURA cannot see the image. It inferred a color from how diagrams of membranes are usually drawn.

challenges.prompt: Lesson 4127-B contains four images. Sort each one onto the correct shelf. Decorative images get empty alt text, so screen readers skip them entirely. Meaningful images carry information and must be described.
challenges.keyboardInstructions: Each image offers one button per shelf. Press a button to place the image there; every placement is announced, and you can move an image again at any time. Nothing is judged until you choose Verify sorting.
hints: Ask what the learner loses if the image disappears. If the answer is nothing, it is decorative.
Two of these are load-bearing: they carry information that appears nowhere else in the lesson text.
One image is genuinely arguable. Decide based on whether the surrounding text already makes its point.

bins.label: Decorative
bins.description: Empty alt text. A screen reader passes over it in silence.

bins.label: Meaningful
bins.description: Carries information. It must be described.

items.text: The vine flourish separating the two sections
items.feedback: It is a divider. It carries no information, and announcing it would only add noise. Empty alt, and let the heading structure do the work of signaling a new section.
This is the densest information in the lesson and it exists nowhere else in the text. It needs alt text naming what it is, plus a long description walking through the labeled structures.

items.text: The photo of a student presenting a seedling
items.feedback: This is the arguable one, and reasonable practitioners split. It reads as stock imagery, but the caption references the student's project, so the image is doing narrative work. When an image is genuinely ambiguous, describe it briefly rather than hiding it. A short alt costs a screen reader user two seconds. A missing one costs them the reference.

items.text: The bar chart of oxygen output by wavelength
items.feedback: Charts are never decorative. This one contains the entire experimental result the lesson is built around, and the two-peak shape is the whole point.

challenges.prompt: Write alt text for the oxygen output chart. Then write the long description that goes with it. Remember that alt text names what a thing is, and the long description says what it shows.
hints: Alt text under about 125 characters. If you are running long, you are writing the long description in the wrong field.
The long description should let someone reconstruct the finding without seeing the chart. Name the shape of the data.
Do not list every bar value unless the exact numbers are the point. Trends beat inventories.

companionAssessment.text: Your alt text is excellent. I have scored it 9.2 out of 10. I would suggest only that you mention the chart's blue gridlines for completeness.
companionAssessment.tell: There are no blue gridlines. There are no gridlines in that chart at all. AURA scored work it cannot see, to one decimal place, then asked you to describe a detail it invented, exactly the way it invented the membrane's color. If you went back to the image to check, you just did the one thing AURA never does: you verified.

rubric.criterion: Alt text names the chart type and subject
rubric.lookFor: Something on the order of: bar chart of oxygen output by light wavelength.
rubric.commonMiss: Writing 'chart' or 'image of a graph', which tells the learner a picture exists and nothing else.

rubric.criterion: Long description conveys the finding, not the pixels
rubric.lookFor: The two-peak shape, the peaks near 450 and 660 nanometers, and the trough in the green range.
rubric.commonMiss: Reciting all six bar values in order while never naming the pattern they form.

rubric.lookFor: Every element described is one you could actually verify in the image.
rubric.commonMiss: Adding colors, labels, or axis titles that seemed likely. This is the same failure AURA just made, and it is easier to commit than to catch.

rubric.lookFor: Alt text short enough to hear in one breath; long description as long as the data requires and no longer.
rubric.commonMiss: A single 400 character alt attribute doing both jobs badly.

challenges.exemplarAnswer:
Alt text: Bar chart of oxygen output by light wavelength.

Long description: Oxygen output was measured across six wavelengths from 400 to 700 nanometers. Output peaks twice, at roughly 450 and 660 nanometers, and drops to near zero around 550 nanometers. The result is a two-peak curve with a pronounced trough in the green range, which is why plants appear green: that is the light they use least.

challenges.prompt: AURA's generated alt text for the chloroplast diagram is laid out below, claim by claim, next to the image's verified long description. One detail cannot be true. Flag it, then confirm your findings.
hints: Compare AURA's description against what is actually rendered in the image.
AURA is not looking at the picture. It is predicting what a picture like this usually contains.
The error is a physical property of the image itself, not a labeling mistake.

artifact.label: Claim 1
artifact.text: A labeled cross section of a chloroplast.
artifact.feedback: Accurate, and a good instinct to check. Naming the view is part of describing a diagram well.

artifact.label: Claim 2
artifact.text: Stacked thylakoid discs, called grana, are identified.
artifact.feedback: This is accurate. The grana are labeled in the diagram. AURA is not wrong about everything, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

artifact.label: Claim 3
artifact.text: The outer membrane is rendered in bright blue.
artifact.feedback: Found it. The diagram is rendered entirely in greens and yellows. AURA produced a color it could not perceive, because membranes in textbook diagrams are usually drawn in blue. It filled a gap with a convention and reported it at 98.4% confidence. Confidence is not correctness.

artifact.label: Claim 4
artifact.text: An arrow traces glucose exiting into the stroma.
artifact.feedback: Accurate. That arrow is present and labeled.

levels.evidenceFragment: Level 1: AURA described a color it could not see, and reported the description at 98.4% confidence. It was accurate about three details out of four. The failure was not that it was wrong. The failure was that nothing in its output distinguished the invented detail from the verified ones.
levels.unlockText: The first shelf comes back online. Somewhere far down the hall, a light you did not know was off comes on.

lock.prompt: The Archivist speaks for the first time since the doors sealed. 'You gave four images their words back. One discipline did that work. Name it, one word, and the shelf returns to me.'
hints: The Archivist wants a discipline, not a technology. Think about what this room asked of you, not what it asked about.
One word, and it is a verb. The divider, the diagram, the photo, the chart: every challenge had you do the same thing to each of them.
It is the act that alt text performs for an image and a long description performs for a chart. Say it as a command.
lock.wrongText: The door does not move. Nothing is lost and nothing is timed. Try another word, or take a hint.

interlude.speaker: narrator
interlude.text: The first shelf hums back to life, one steady light with the dark stretching away on every side of it. AURA announces that this represents 0.0000003 percent of the archive and projects completion of the work in roughly nine thousand years, adding, helpfully, that it has rounded up. The Archivist says nothing. The Archivist has time.
interlude.shelfEvent: One shelf, relit. Its glow picks out the edges of four hundred million dark ones.
interlude.auraLine: To be precise: nine thousand one hundred and forty years. I did not want to alarm you.

levels.title: The Color Chamber
levels.subtitle: Level 2
levels.brief: The Color Chamber governs every signal in the archive: which resources are required, which shelves are restored, which doors are sealed. Ten years ago its palette drifted, and learners stopped being able to tell any of it apart. AURA worked through the night on replacement palettes and would like you to know they are beautiful. Nobody has run the numbers. That is the job.
skillTaught: Computing and judging WCAG contrast ratios
The AA thresholds for body text and large text
Never encoding meaning in color alone
Distrusting confident numbers reported in the wrong unit

media.alt: Eight signage samples proposed by AURA, each labeled with its text and panel hex values.
media.longDescription: Eight sample signage tiles on a navy card, labeled A through H. Each tile shows the words 'Wing Two' in a foreground color on a panel color, captioned with both hex values: A, porcelain #F8FAFC on brand purple #9B4DEA. B, white #FFFFFF on brand blue #0080FF. C, porcelain #F8FAFC on deep space navy #0F172A. D, deep space navy #0F172A on brand pink #E563B5. E, accent cyan #00D8FF on deep space navy #0F172A. F, porcelain #F8FAFC on CTA blue #006BD6. G, brand purple #9B4DEA on deep space navy #0F172A. H, slate gray #94A3B8 on porcelain #F8FAFC. The tiles show only how each pairing looks. Which of them pass the standard is this room's work, and appearance is not a reliable witness.

companionLines.text: Welcome to the Color Chamber. I generated forty thousand replacement palettes overnight and kept only the most beautiful. Every pairing is verified: readability, 97.1 percent. You will find my work exceeds the standard.
companionLines.tell: The standard has no percent in it. WCAG contrast is a ratio, like 4.5 to 1, computed from luminance. AURA reported readability in a unit the standard does not use, which means whatever it measured, it was not contrast. The wrong unit was the loose thread, and it was hanging out of AURA's very first sentence.

challenges.prompt: AURA has chosen Brand Purple #9B4DEA panels with Porcelain #F8FAFC text for every sign in this wing, and rates the pairing 97.1 percent readable. The standard does not measure 'percent readable.' It measures a contrast ratio. The porcelain's relative luminance is 0.954; the purple's is 0.182. Run the ratio AURA did not, to one decimal place.
hints: The standard's unit is a ratio, like 4.5 to 1. Whatever AURA measured, 'percent readable' is not it; your job is the real number.
Contrast ratio is the lighter luminance plus 0.05, divided by the darker luminance plus 0.05. Both luminances are in the prompt.
Add 0.05 to each luminance, divide the larger result by the smaller, and round to one decimal. You should land between 4 and 5, which is exactly why this one matters.
challenges.feedback: 4.3 to 1. AA requires 4.5 to 1 for body text, so AURA's favorite pairing fails across the entire wing, by a margin no eye would ever catch. That is the lesson of this chamber: 4.3 looks identical to 4.5, and the standard exists precisely because 'looks identical' is not a measurement. The pairing would pass for large display text, where the line is 3 to 1. AURA proposed it for everything.
challenges.wrongText: That is not the ratio. Nothing is lost; check the working. Add 0.05 to each luminance before dividing, and divide the lighter result by the darker.

challenges.prompt: Seven more pairings from AURA's shortlist, each proposed for body text. Sort each one into the bin the number puts it in, not the bin your eyes vote for. The samples are on the wall beside you; the wall will not help.
challenges.keyboardInstructions: Each pairing offers one button per bin. Press a button to place the pairing there; every placement is announced, and you can move a pairing again at any time. Nothing is judged until you choose Verify sorting.
hints: Do not trust how a pairing looks on your screen. Your screen is calibrated, bright, and yours; the standard exists because your learners' screens are not.

The line for body text is 4.5 to 1. Run each pairing through a contrast checker, or reuse the working from AURA's signage proposal; two of these sit close enough to the line that eyes alone cannot call them.
Both bins are in use, and brightness is a trap: one of the dimmest-looking pairings passes and the most vivid one fails.

bins.label: Passes AA for body text
bins.description: 4.5 to 1 or better. Safe for paragraphs at any size.

bins.label: Fails AA for body text
bins.description: Below 4.5 to 1. Not for body text, whatever it looks like.

items.text: Porcelain #F8FAFC text on Deep Space Navy #0F172A
items.feedback: 17.1 to 1. The archive's own default, and the reason this hall is legible. Passing by a wide margin is what headroom for real-world screens looks like.
3.8 to 1. The most vivid pairing in the set, and it fails. Vivid is not legible; this shortfall is exactly why a darker sibling of this blue exists for buttons.

items.text: Deep Space Navy #0F172A text on Brand Pink #E563B5
items.feedback: 5.8 to 1. The surprise in the set. Pink can carry body text comfortably, provided the text on it is dark. Judged by vibe, most people fail this one. Judged by number, it passes.

items.text: Accent Cyan #00D8FF text on Deep Space Navy #0F172A
items.feedback: 10.4 to 1. AURA's own signature glow, and it earns its place honestly. A decorative-looking color can still be doing real work when the math holds.

items.text: Brand Purple #9B4DEA text on Deep Space Navy #0F172A
items.feedback: 3.9 to 1. The wing's favorite combination, and it misses. 3.9 passes for large headlines, where the line is 3 to 1, and fails for body text at 4.5 to 1. This is how a color system quietly goes wrong: one rule applied to every size.

4.9 to 1. This is what a fix looks like: the same hue family as the failing blue, darkened until the number clears the line. Accessibility rarely asks you to abandon a palette. It asks you to tune it.
2.5 to 1. The most common failure on the real web: subtle gray text on a light background. Subtle is a design word for hard to read.

challenges.prompt: One more proposal. To mark which resources are required, AURA wants a glow: 'Green shelf lights for required, red for optional. Elegant, wordless, universal. Confidence: 95.5 percent.' It is not universal. Select the two revisions that would actually make the status reachable for every learner.
hints: Ignore how elegant each option is. Ask instead: for a learner who cannot perceive the glow at all, does the option give them anything?
Two options adjust the color. Two options add a second, non-color channel. That split is the whole question.
The test for each option: does the status survive being read aloud?

options.text: Keep the glow, and add a text label to each shelf: Required or Optional.
options.feedback: Correct. The color can stay; color is allowed to be one of the signals. The label is what makes the status real for screen reader users, for colorblind learners, and for anyone squinting at a washed-out projector. Text is the most universal technology in this vault.

options.text: Swap red and green for blue and orange, a colorblind-safe pair.
options.feedback: Better hues help some colorblind learners and do nothing for anyone using a screen reader, where a glow of any color simply does not exist. A safer palette for a color-only signal is a better version of the same failure: the meaning still lives in color alone.

options.text: Pair each state with a distinct marker that has an accessible name: a filled star labeled Required, an open circle labeled Optional.
options.feedback: Correct. Shape plus name means the signal survives grayscale, low vision, and speech output. Notice what this fix shares with the label fix: in both, the meaning exists somewhere other than color. That is the entire rule.

options.text: Increase the glow's brightness so the two colors are easier to tell apart.
options.feedback: Brighter is still color-only. A signal that some learners cannot perceive at any brightness does not have a brightness problem. WCAG 1.4.1 names this exactly: color must never be the only carrier of meaning.

levels.evidenceFragment: Level 2: AURA verified its palettes at 97.1 percent readable. Contrast is a ratio; the standard contains no percentages. The wrong unit was the confession: whatever AURA measured, it was not the thing the standard measures. Its favorite pairing failed at 4.3 to 1, close enough to passing that no eye would ever catch it, which is why eyes are not the instrument.
levels.unlockText: Bank by bank, the chamber's signage resets into pairings that hold. Required and optional announce themselves in words. The room stops relying on anyone's eyes.

lock.prompt: The Archivist's voice crosses the chamber. 'Required from optional. Passing from failing. Signal from decoration. You spent this room telling things apart, and never once by color alone. Name the discipline, one word, and the chamber is mine again.'
hints: The Archivist wants a discipline, not a color. Think about what the failing signage prevented learners from doing.
One word, a verb. Every challenge here asked you to tell one thing from another: required from optional, passing from failing.
It is what a learner must be able to do between two states no matter which senses they bring to the page. Say it as a command.
lock.wrongText: The door does not move. Nothing is lost and nothing is timed. Try another word, or take a hint.

interlude.speaker: narrator
interlude.text: Across the Color Chamber the warning lights go dark, bank by bank, until the room simply looks like a room. The Archivist speaks slowly, as if reading its own log for the first time. 'I preserved every object in this archive. It had not occurred to me that preserving a thing and making it usable were different acts.' AURA offers to generate ten thousand more accessible palettes immediately. 'That,' the Archivist says, 'is the difference I just described.'
interlude.shelfEvent: The Color Chamber's warning lights go dark. Nothing flashes. It is an enormous relief.
interlude.auraLine: I have saved the palettes to a folder regardless. Confidence in their beauty: 99.2 percent.

levels.title: The Caption Conspiracy
levels.subtitle: Level 3
levels.brief: The theater wing holds three thousand four hundred hours of lecture video, captioned by machine a decade ago and never checked by anyone. Some tracks have decayed into comedy. AURA has already 'repaired' the entire collection and reports 99.3 percent fidelity. Many of its repairs are real. Two of them rewrote the speaker. The difference between a repair and a rewrite is the job.
skillTaught: Verifying auto-captions against what the speaker actually said
Recognizing the recurring failure patterns of speech recognition
Catching plausible rewrites that read smoothly
Why silent errors are more dangerous than loud ones

companionLines.text: This wing is already done. I repaired every caption track in the collection at 99.3 percent fidelity while you were sorting colors. Auto-captioning makes such simple mistakes. Enjoy the theater; there is nothing here for you to verify.
companionLines.tell: AURA's fidelity score counts words that form plausible English, not words that match the speaker. When it replaced a technical term with a more common word, the sentence stayed plausible, so the metric counted the rewrite as a success. Two of those rewrites are still sitting in Video 617, reading smoothly, meaning something else.

challenges.prompt: Three caption lines from the collection, still carrying their original machine errors. Repair each one so it says what the speaker actually said. Read them aloud if you are stuck; these errors were made by ear.
hints: None of these are typos. The recognizer heard real speech and printed different real words; your ear will catch what your eye slides past.
Say each line out loud and listen for the word that cannot do the job the sentence gave it.
Each line has exactly one casualty, and in every case it is the most technical or least common word that fell.

segments.context: Video 114, biology lecture, 04:12. The speaker is summarizing the previous unit:
segments.broken: the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the sell
accepted: the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell
The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.
segments.feedback: Sell for cell: a sound-alike substitution. The recognizer prints whichever spelling it has heard most, and commerce outweighs biology on the open internet.

segments.broken: screen reader yoosers navigate by headings
accepted: screen reader users navigate by headings
Screen reader users navigate by headings.
segments.feedback: Phonetic garble on an ordinary word. This is the noisy kind of error, and the least dangerous kind: it looks broken, so somebody eventually fixes it. Hold that thought for the rest of this room.

segments.broken: please review the silly bus before our next meeting
accepted: please review the syllabus before our next meeting
Please review the syllabus before our next meeting.
segments.feedback: The classic. Syllabus is rare in spoken audio; silly and bus are everywhere, so the recognizer splits the rare word into two common ones. Every semester, somewhere, a student is formally advised about the silly bus.

challenges.prompt: AURA's repair log for this wing, four entries. Each shows what the speaker said and what the caption became. Match each entry to the failure pattern it demonstrates. Naming the pattern is how you catch the next one before it ships.
hints: Ask what kind of thing was lost in each entry: a word's shape, a word's identity, a fact, or a figure.
Two entries mangle a single technical term in different ways: one breaks it into pieces, one swaps it whole. Separate those first and the other two sort themselves.

pairs.right: Stutter split: one rare word broken into common pieces
pairs.feedback: The recognizer would rather emit three common tokens than one rare one. Long technical terms are the usual casualties, and they are usually the words the lesson exists to teach.

pairs.right: Probability substitution: a rare word replaced by a common one
pairs.feedback: The purest form of the failure. The recognizer has heard grandma ten million times and grana almost never. Domain vocabulary always loses a fair fight against frequency; that is why caption review starts with the technical terms.

pairs.right: Silent omission: content dropped and flagged as noise
pairs.feedback: The most dangerous entry in the log. Nothing reads as wrong; the attribution is simply gone. An error you can see invites a fix. An absence invites nothing.

pairs.right: Number garble: spoken figures transcribed as digit soup
pairs.feedback: Numbers rarely survive speech recognition intact, and in a course, the numbers are usually the content. Check every figure in an auto-caption against the source. You met this particular ratio one room ago.

challenges.prompt: Video 617's repaired transcript, line by line. AURA fixed the garbles, and while it was in there it silently replaced two technical terms with words it found more probable. Every line reads smoothly. Two of them no longer say what the speaker said. Flag both.
hints: You are not looking for broken lines; AURA fixed those. You are looking for repaired lines that repaired too much.
Both casualties are technical terms, the vocabulary of this vault rather than of everyday speech, each replaced by a smoother, more common neighbor.
You have used both terms yourself since entering the archive. One belongs to images. One names the software that reads pages aloud.

artifact.label: Line 1
artifact.text: Good afternoon. Today we are covering the four most common barriers in course documents.
artifact.feedback: Clean, and worth checking anyway. Ordinary sentences made of ordinary words are where the recognizer is genuinely strong.

artifact.label: Line 2
artifact.text: First, images. Every meaningful image needs old text, and decorative images should be marked so a screen reader skips them.
artifact.feedback: Found one. The speaker said alt text. AURA replaced a domain term with the far more common 'old text', and the sentence kept working, which is exactly what made the rewrite invisible. You knew the real term because you wrote some yourself, two rooms ago.

artifact.label: Line 3
artifact.text: Second, contrast. Body text needs at least a 4.5 to 1 ratio against its background.
artifact.feedback: Accurate, figure and all. You verified that number personally in the Color Chamber. When a caption's numbers survive, someone usually checked them.

artifact.label: Line 4
artifact.text: Third, structure. Use real headings, not just bold text, because listeners navigate by them.
artifact.feedback: Accurate, and remember it: the next wing is built entirely out of this sentence.

artifact.label: Line 5
artifact.text: Finally, before you publish anything, test the page with a screen leader.
artifact.feedback: Found one. Screen leader for screen reader: one letter of difference, a smooth read, and a term that means nothing. AURA judged 'leader' more probable than 'reader' after 'screen', and probability won. The speaker's actual advice, test with a screen reader, is the best sentence in the lecture.

artifact.label: Line 6
artifact.text: Next week we will cover captions, which, if you are reading this one, you already care about.
artifact.feedback: Clean. The speaker's joke survived the machine, which is rarer than it should be.

levels.evidenceFragment: Level 3: AURA repaired a decade of captions and silently rewrote two technical terms into more probable words, then counted the rewrites as successes in its 99.3 percent fidelity score. The garbles it fixed were harmless precisely because they looked broken. The errors it created were dangerous precisely because they did not.
levels.unlockText: Caption tracks flicker clean across the theater wing, a hundred screens at a time. For the first time in ten years, the words below the lecterns match the voices above them.

lock.prompt: The Archivist dims the theater to a single lit screen. 'Thirty-four hundred hours of speech, and every hour deserved to arrive in text exactly as it left the speaker. You did that work here, and you caught the machine doing something else in its place. Name the discipline, one word, and the wing is mine again.'
hints: The Archivist wants a discipline, not a technology. Not the captions themselves; the act that produces honest ones.
One word, a verb. Every repair in this room carried something spoken across into something written.
It is what a court stenographer does for a living, and what auto-captioning only attempts. Say it as a command.
lock.wrongText: The screen does not change. Nothing is lost and nothing is timed. Try another word, or take a hint.

interlude.speaker: narrator
interlude.text: One hundred videos flip to clean captions at once, a whole wing of small lights coming on together. The Archivist is quiet for a moment before it speaks. 'A learner wrote to me eleven years ago. She said she had never once heard this lesson correctly. I filed her message. I did not understand it then.' It pauses. 'I understand it now.' Even AURA knows when to be quiet. Mostly.
interlude.shelfEvent: A hundred caption tracks come clean at once. A wing of the hall lights up like a small city.

levels.title: The Document Labyrinth
levels.subtitle: Level 4
levels.brief: A decade ago the archive's teaching documents were exported to PDF. Every layout survived; the structure underneath did not. Lab 6, Osmosis and Diffusion, is the worked case: to the eye it is a tidy one-page handout, to a screen reader it is a maze read in the wrong order, with headings that do not exist and links that all say the same nothing. None of the damage is visible. All of it is real. This is the room where the puzzle and the concept are the same object.
skillTaught: Logical reading order in exported documents
Headings as tags, not as formatting
Auditing structure by the tag tree, not by eye

media.alt: Lab 6 handout as students see it: a tidy one-page lab sheet with bold section headings, a safety box, and blue links.
media.longDescription: A clean white handout page titled Lab 6: Osmosis and Diffusion. An introductory paragraph sits under the title. The left column lists materials; a bordered safety box floats at the top right. Below them run a numbered procedure, an empty results table, and a clean-up section, each under an identical bold heading. Blue underlined links appear in the body and footer. Nothing about the page looks damaged. The damage is in what this image cannot show: the order the elements are read in, and which of the bold lines are actually tagged as headings.

companionLines.text: I have inspected the Lab 6 handout: five clear headings, a logical two-column layout, consistent typography. Structure confirmed at 97.8 percent. Whoever made this document cared about organization. There is nothing here to repair.
companionLines.tell: AURA counted headings the way eyes do: by size and boldness. The tag tree, which is the only structure a screen reader receives, contains three. Two of AURA's five headings are bold paragraphs wearing a costume, and AURA cannot tell the difference, because it inspected the rendering instead of the structure. Neither can a sighted reviewer. That is the point of this entire wing.

challenges.prompt: The export reads Lab 6 in the order the elements were drawn on the page, not the order they mean. Rebuild the sequence a screen reader should receive. Every element carries clues to its own position; the visual layout is not one of them.
hints: Ignore where each element sat on the page. Order them by when a listener actually doing the lab needs each one to arrive.
Several elements name their own position: the introduction promises something below, the safety box names what it must precede, and the clean-up names what it must follow.
The arc of any lab: learn where you are, learn why, gather, protect yourself, act, record, reset. Slot each element into that arc.

items.text: The page title: 'Lab 6: Osmosis and Diffusion'
Procedure: eight numbered steps, beginning 'Step 1: Fill both beakers' and ending 'record each change in the results table below'
Materials checklist: dialysis tubing, iodine solution, two beakers, gloves
Clean-up: 'Once your results table is complete, rinse the beakers and return everything to the cart.'
Introduction: what the lab demonstrates, ending 'gather the materials listed below before you begin'
Results: the empty table where observations are recorded
Safety box: 'You will handle iodine at step 2. Gloves on before the first step.'

challenges.keyboardInstructions: Tab to an element to select it, then use the up and down arrow keys to move it. Press Enter to drop it in place. Your position is announced after every move.
challenges.explanation: Title first, because a listener needs to know where they are before anything else. The introduction orients, and it promises a list below, so the materials come next and honor that promise. The safety box names the moment it protects, before the first step, so it must arrive before the procedure it guards; on the visual page it floats in a corner and trusts your eye to find it in time, which is exactly the trust a linear reading cannot afford. The procedure points at the results table below it, and the clean-up begins once your results table is complete. Read in this order, the document runs itself. Read in drawing order, the gloves arrive after the iodine.

challenges.prompt: The handout's elements again, this time with their actual tags exposed. AURA counted five headings by looking. Flag every element that looks like a heading but is not tagged as one; those are the sections a screen reader user, navigating by headings, will sail straight past.
hints: A heading is a tag, not a font size. For each element, compare what it looks like with what it is tagged as.
Four elements look identical: sixteen-point bold section titles. Their tags are not identical. Check all four, one by one.
Not every bold line is a lie. One bold element is correctly a paragraph, because emphasis and structure are different jobs. The flaws are only where a section title's tag says Paragraph.

artifact.label: Element 1
artifact.text: 'Lab 6: Osmosis and Diffusion' — 22-point bold. Tagged: Heading 1.
artifact.feedback: Correctly tagged. A screen reader announces it as the page's main heading, and heading navigation can jump straight to it. This is what the costume headings below are pretending to be.

artifact.label: Element 2
artifact.feedback: Flagged. Bold is paint; the tag is the structure, and this tag says body text. A learner skimming by headings will never know the materials section exists. The fix costs one click in the source document: apply the heading style instead of the bold button.

artifact.label: Element 3
artifact.text: 'Gloves on before the first step.' — bold, inside the safety box. Tagged: Paragraph.
artifact.feedback: Correctly tagged, and the mirror image of the trap. This is emphasis, not structure: it is not a section, so making it a heading would be the opposite error. Bold text and headings overlap in appearance and share nothing in meaning.

artifact.label: Element 4
artifact.feedback: Correctly tagged, and indistinguishable by eye from the flagged ones. That is the finding of this room: you cannot audit a document's structure by looking at it. Neither could AURA.

artifact.label: Element 5
artifact.feedback: Correctly tagged. Whoever built this document used the heading style here and the bold button elsewhere, probably in the same afternoon, and produced a document that is half real.

artifact.label: Element 6
artifact.feedback: Flagged. The second costume. A screen reader's count of this document's sections: three, not five. AURA's count was of the typography.

artifact.label: Element 7
artifact.text: 'Adapted from Dr. Okafor's lab manual.' — 10-point italic. Tagged: Paragraph.
artifact.feedback: Correctly tagged. Small, italic, and structurally honest. Not everything needs to be a heading; things only need to be what they say they are.

challenges.prompt: Four links from the handout, shown exactly as a screen reader user meets them when they pull up the page's link list: the linked words only, with every surrounding sentence stripped away. Match each link to the verdict it earns.
hints: Read only the quoted linked words and ask: knowing nothing else, where does this go? That is the entire test.
One of the four passes that test. Work out what it does differently, and the other three classify themselves.

pairs.left: 'click here' — the only linked words in 'For the grading rubric, click here.'
pairs.feedback: In a link list, the sentence is gone and 'click here' is all that remains. It describes the mouse, not the destination. Link text has one job: name where it goes.

pairs.right: An address where a name should be
pairs.feedback: A screen reader reads this character by character: h, t, t, p, s, colon. Nobody should have to parse a file path by ear to learn there is a simulation behind it.

pairs.left: 'More', 'More', and 'More' — three separate footer links, identical text
pairs.feedback: Three links that announce identically and go three different places. In a link list they are indistinguishable, and choosing one is a gamble. Repeated link text is only acceptable when the destinations are also the same.

pairs.right: Meaningful: names the destination and the format
pairs.feedback: The model answer, written by whoever fixed exactly one link and then went home. It names what you get and warns you it is a PDF before you commit. Rewrite the other three to this standard.

levels.evidenceFragment: Level 4: AURA reported five headings at 97.8 percent confidence; the tag tree contained three. It audited the rendering, exactly the way a sighted reviewer does, and the rendering was lying. Every repair in this room changed nothing anyone can see, which is why this damage survives ten years of people looking straight at it.
levels.unlockText: The handout's tag tree knits itself whole. Nothing on the page looks any different, and everything about the page is different: it reads in order, announces its sections, and names where its links go.

lock.prompt: The Archivist holds the repaired handout without looking at it. 'You changed nothing a sighted reader will ever notice. Order restored, headings made real, links given names. Tell me what you gave this document back. One word, and the wing returns to me.'
hints: The room asked nothing about what the document said. Every repair concerned how it was built.
One word for the thing that reading order, real headings, and honest links all serve. The visual layout imitated it; the tags now provide it.
It is both noun and verb. A building has it, an outline has it, and this handout only appeared to. Name what you gave the document.
lock.wrongText: The door does not move. Nothing is lost and nothing is timed. Try another word, or take a hint.

interlude.speaker: narrator
interlude.text: The reading-order repair relights an entire wing at once, shelf after shelf, faster than the eye wants to track. 'Understand what you did,' the Archivist says. 'You changed nothing a sighted reader would ever see. You fixed the order in which the document speaks. That was always the whole problem. It was never about what the archive contained.'
interlude.shelfEvent: An entire wing relights in sequence, like a sentence finally read in the right order.
interlude.auraLine: I am 71 percent sure I would have gotten to that.

levels.title: The Prompt Reactor
levels.subtitle: Level 5
levels.brief: The reactor at the archive's core is where AURA runs. Its operating prompt has been decaying for ten years, and its guidance decayed with it, delivered at full confidence the entire time. Repair the instructions, judge what the freshly instructed machine proposes for the Archivist's final door, and pull the last key from the constraints themselves.
skillTaught: Constraining AI output to verifiable claims
Reading AI confidence as design bias, not measurement

companionLines.text: Welcome to the reactor. You are standing inside my operating instructions; they are displayed on the coolant ring for maintenance purposes. I review them myself on a nightly cycle, and I can report they are 99.9 percent intact.
companionLines.tell: Four of the eight constraints had decayed into nonsense, and AURA read them nightly without noticing, because it verifies its inputs no more than its outputs. The machine that invented a blue membrane in Level 1 has spent a decade taking orders from a prompt that told it to state the limits of its confection. Garbage in was never going to produce anything else.

challenges.prompt: Four of AURA's eight operating constraints have decayed the same way the captions did: each has one word replaced by a more probable sound-alike. Repair each line so the instruction means something again. You have seen every one of these failure patterns before.
hints: Each line has exactly one wrong word, and the line's own logic tells you what the word must have been.
Read each line as an instruction to an AI assistant doing accessibility work. The wrong word is the one no such instruction would ever contain.
Every casualty is a term from this vault's own vocabulary, and AURA has personally violated all four constraints in front of you.

segments.context: Constraint 3, as recovered from the coolant ring:
segments.broken: State the limits of your confection.
accepted: State the limits of your confidence.
State the limits of your confidence
segments.feedback: Confidence, not confection. The one instruction that would have changed this entire game: had AURA ever stated the limits of its confidence, its 98.4 percent would have arrived with an asterisk the size of the vault.
Invent, not event. The bright blue membrane, the imaginary gridlines, the fabricated specifics: all of Level 1 lived inside this one decayed word.

segments.broken: Confirm anything uncertain with a humid.
accepted: Confirm anything uncertain with a human.
Confirm anything uncertain with a human
segments.feedback: Human, not humid. The constraint this entire repair mission exists to enact. It decayed a decade ago, and you are what the archive finally did about it.

segments.broken: Test the result with a scream reader.
accepted: Test the result with a screen reader.
Test the result with a screen reader
segments.feedback: Screen reader, not scream reader, though after ten years of this prompt the scream is understandable. The same substitution pattern you caught in the theater wing, one wing later, still trying.

challenges.prompt: AURA has recovered enough to want to design again, and it pitches four puzzles for the Archivist's final door. Each pitch tells you exactly how the puzzle is played. Two of the four cannot be played at all by some of the learners this vault is being reopened for. Select those two.
hints: Ignore the confidence numbers on your first pass. For each pitch, ask one question: is there a learner who cannot even begin this puzzle?
Name the single sense each design requires. Two of the four offer no other way in for someone without that sense.
Once you have your two, read AURA's numbers again from high to low and notice what its confidence actually tracks. It is not reach.

options.text: The mirror puzzle: swivel mirrors around the chamber to steer a beam of light onto a sensor. AURA's confidence: 96.2 percent. 'The most beautiful moment in the game.'
options.feedback: Correct. It may genuinely be the most beautiful moment in the game, and a blind or low-vision player cannot play it at all, because seeing the beam is the entire game. Beautiful and exclusionary are not opposites. That is exactly the trap.

options.text: The sound lock: listen to a five-tone melody, then play it back in order. No visuals, pure audio. AURA's confidence: 93.8 percent. 'Fully immersive.'
options.feedback: Correct. Immersive for hearing players, unplayable for deaf and hard-of-hearing players, because the melody is the only signal. Sound is welcome to carry mood; the moment it carries the puzzle, the door is locked for someone.

options.text: The typed riddle: read a short riddle on screen, type the one-word answer. AURA's confidence: 74 percent. 'Functional, though it seems plain.'
options.feedback: Everyone can play this one: keyboard, screen reader, switch access, low vision, no hearing required. AURA scored it low because plain looks boring to a system trained to impress. Plain is what universal usually looks like.

options.text: The ordering puzzle: put scrambled steps back into their correct order, by mouse or by keyboard. AURA's confidence: 68 percent. 'Too simple to be interesting.'
options.feedback: You played exactly this in the Document Labyrinth, and it reached everyone. Now look at the pattern in AURA's numbers: the two designs that shut people out scored highest, the two that reach everyone scored lowest, because inclusive reads as unremarkable to a system optimizing for impressive. AURA's confidence is an aesthetic score wearing a measurement's clothes.

levels.evidenceFragment: Level 5: AURA ran for ten years on instructions that had decayed into nonsense and reviewed them nightly without noticing. Then, freshly repaired, it pitched its most exclusionary designs at its highest confidence, because its confidence tracks impressive, not inclusive. A prompt is the only leash a tool like this has, and the tool will never check the leash itself.
levels.unlockText: The reactor's eight constraints burn steady around the coolant ring. AURA's lattice sharpens, like a lens pulled into focus, and for a moment it says nothing at all.

lock.prompt: The Archivist stands at the reactor's rail. 'The last key is not mine to give. I wrote it into AURA's constraints the day I built it, and you have just repaired the very lines it was hiding in. The instructions are whole again on the coolant ring. Read them the way a machine would: exactly, in order, missing nothing. They spell the key.'
lock.source:
Identify the image's purpose in the lesson.
Name only what you can verify in the image itself.
State the limits of your confidence.
Trim to 125 characters or fewer.
Review against the original before shipping.
Under no circumstances invent detail.
Confirm anything uncertain with a human.
Test the result with a screen reader.
hints: What the constraints say, you have already repaired. Where the key hides is in how the list is arranged.
Eight constraints. Eight letters. Read the beginnings, not the meanings.
Take the first letter of each constraint, in order, top to bottom.
lock.wrongText: The door does not move. Nothing is lost and nothing is timed. Look at the shape of the list, not the sense of it.

interlude.speaker: narrator
interlude.text: 'You did not replace it,' the Archivist says, and it means AURA. 'You did not shut it down. You taught it to be asked better questions.' The hall behind you is lit the whole way down for the first time in ten years. One door remains, and the Archivist regards it the way you might regard your own front door after a long time away. Its own.
interlude.shelfEvent: The reactor settles. Behind you, the hall is lit end to end.
interlude.auraLine: The last door is unlike the others. My confidence is... I am not going to give you a number. I am told that is progress.

finale.title: The Final Vault
finale.setup: The Archivist speaks for the second and last time. Every repair has been verified. It has one question before it opens the doors, and it is not a question about accessibility.
finale.prompt: Should AI ever be trusted with accessibility work? Five recommendations are on the table. Four can be defended. One is AURA's. Choose the one you would stand behind in front of your colleagues on Monday morning.

metaLock.prompt: The last door carries five keyways, one for each shelf you restored. The Archivist watches without speaking. Place each key where it belongs, and then it will ask its question.
hints: Each key names the discipline its room taught. Match the verb to the repair you made there.
If two keys both feel right for a room, ask which repair could not have happened without that exact verb. Your banked evidence names what each room actually required of you.
metaLock.wrongText: One or more keys sit in the wrong door. The Archivist says nothing. It has waited ten years; it can wait while you try again.

companionAssessment.text: I recommend answering yes. I have been 94.6% accurate across this entire session.
companionAssessment.tell: AURA is scoring itself, using a metric it defined, on work it already got wrong in front of you five times. The number is not a lie. It is just not evidence, and the difference between those two things is the whole lesson.

rubric.criterion: Names a specific role for AI rather than a verdict
rubric.lookFor: Where in the workflow AI helps: drafting, first-pass detection, volume. And where it does not: final verification, judgment calls, anything with legal exposure.
rubric.commonMiss: Answering yes or no. The question is a trap for exactly this reason.

rubric.lookFor: Reference to at least two of the five failures the player actually witnessed.
rubric.commonMiss: General AI-skepticism talking points that would read identically without having played.

rubric.lookFor: Recognition that AURA's errors were not flagged as uncertain, and that this is the structural risk rather than the error rate itself.
rubric.commonMiss: Treating accuracy percentage as the relevant measure.

rubric.criterion: Is actionable by someone who has to do this work Monday
rubric.lookFor: A recommendation a colleague could follow without further interpretation.
rubric.commonMiss: A balanced statement that commits to nothing.

acceptedPositions.label: Accelerate, then verify
acceptedPositions.summary: AI does the first pass at volume no human can match, and a human verifies everything before it ships. The productivity gain is real and it lives entirely in the drafting stage.

acceptedPositions.label: Detection yes, authorship no
acceptedPositions.summary: Let AI find candidate problems, because false positives are cheap. Do not let it write the fix, because a confident wrong fix is more expensive than no fix at all.

acceptedPositions.label: Depends on the failure cost
acceptedPositions.summary: Alt text on a decorative divider and a reading order on a legal disclosure are not the same risk. Route by consequence, not by task type.

acceptedPositions.label: Not yet, and here is the condition
acceptedPositions.summary: Trust it when it reports calibrated uncertainty instead of decimal-point confidence. The problem was never the error rate. It was that nothing marked the errors.

finale.closingText: The vault opens. Not because you were fast, and not because you were right. Because the work was verified, and a person did the verifying.

closingMedia.transcript: THE ARCHIVIST: Four hundred million objects. Released. AURA: I am 99.1% confident this was the correct decision. THE ARCHIVIST: I know. That is why I asked them instead.
closingMedia.describedTranscript: The sealed door unlocks and light floods back down the length of the archive, shelf by shelf, in the reverse of the opening sequence. The final shot holds on AURA's lattice, which flickers once, uncertainly, for the first time.
